newsitem.title: POLAND: Zloty seen inching up, testing c.bank patience.
newsitem.headline: Zloty seen inching up, testing c.bank patience.

text.p: The Polish zloty, in central bank intervention territory since Monday, is likely to inch yet higher against the basket of currencies during the day to test where the bank would step in against it, dealers said.
They said many players, anticipating the National Bank of Poland's action against the zloty, were sitting on long dollar positions which they would start winding up once the intervention happened.
"The zloty is likely to keep testing higher and higher ground today because the market wants to know where the NBP would intervene," said Jerzy Wyjadlowski of Bank Slaski SA.

At 0745 GMT the zloty was at 3.13/3.08 percent from the trading band centre against 3.15/3.05 percent at the opening. The NBP has often stopped the zloty's rise already at three percent from the band centre.
Some dealers said the NBP might wait until the end of the day when banks would close the long dollar positions not to keep them over the weekend, and step in only then.

"Banks want to keep higher yielding zloty positions over the weekend so they will have to sell their dollars before the day's end and the NBP might intervene only when they finish -- when it will hurt the most," said Piotr Czyzewski of ING bank.

The zloty has been under upward pressure since Monday, when foreigners started exchanging currencies to pay for T-bills bought at the primary tender. Foreign bids at the auction amounted to $125 million.
Dealers said foreigners were unlikely to be active on the market today, waiting for the outcome of the war of nerves between the NBP and traders.

"For foreigners an NBP intervention weakening the zloty at the end of the day would be a real gift in view of the extra primary T-bill tender on Thursday, in which they are likely to bid," a dealer at a foreign bank here said.
On Thursday the finance ministry is offering 500 million zlotys of its 52-week bills, which enjoyed very high demand at Monday's primary tender after weeks of only small interest.
Call money traded at 23.00/23.50 percent as spreads widened from the morning's 23.20/23.40 percent amid tighter liquidity caused by payments for T-bills bought on Monday.

Dealers did not expect the NBP to drain the market any further. "With rates above 23 percent against the NBP's 14-day reverse repo rate of 22.15, the bank is likely to leave the market alone today," said Piotr Wrobel of Bank Handlowy SA.
